title: How Noise Pollution Changes Our Health
speaker: Ethan Brooks
description: 噪音污染对身心健康被低估的影响
transcript:
Right, imagine you're trying to get to sleep. It's late, the street outside is quiet, and then — boom — a motorbike revs past, or a neighbour's music thumps through the wall. Suddenly you're wide awake, your heart's racing, and you're lying there fuming. Well, tonight I want to talk about why that reaction involves far more than simple annoyance.

I'm Ethan Brooks, and I'm a researcher in public health. Most of my work looks at noise — not the kind you can see, like a rubbish pile, but the kind you only hear. And here's the problem: 'cause it's invisible, we tend to treat it as a minor irritation, kinda. We'll complain about it over dinner and then forget it. But the evidence says we should take it much, much more seriously. Um, I dunno, we just put up with it, don't we?

Let me start with the body. You know, when a loud sound hits you, your brain doesn't wait to check whether it's dangerous. It fires off a sort of stress response straight away — your pulse jumps, your blood pressure climbs, and a hormone called cortisol floods your system. Now, that's fine if a bus is actually about to hit you. But if it's just a lorry going past for the hundredth time, your body still reacts as if there's an emergency. Basically, your system can't tell the difference. It's a physical reaction, not a choice — you can't decide to ignore it, any more than you can decide not to blink when something flies towards your eye. There's a large study — I'm gonna round the figures — that followed people living near busy roads for years, and it found a clear link between constant traffic noise and higher rates of heart disease. I mean, we're talking about the same sort of risk you'd get from, like, smoking or being seriously overweight. That's not nothing.

And here's the sneaky part: it happens while you sleep. You might think, well, I'm asleep, so it doesn't count. But your ears don't switch off. Your brain keeps monitoring the noise all night, and you never reach that deep, proper rest your body needs. So you wake up tired, even though you've been in bed for eight hours. You can't see the damage, and you can't feel it happening, but it builds up, night after night. That's why people who live beside a busy road often describe themselves as permanently exhausted, without ever connecting it to the traffic outside their window.

Now let's look at the mind, because this is where it gets really interesting for me. There was this study of schoolchildren — I think it was near an airport, or maybe a railway — where researchers compared kids in noisy classrooms with kids in quieter ones. And the noisier group were, on average, months behind in reading. Not because they were less clever, but because they couldn't hear clearly and their minds sorta kept drifting off. Every time a plane went over, the teacher's voice vanished for a few seconds, and the kids just lost the thread. Imagine that happening dozens of times a day, every single day. It's like trying to read with someone constantly tapping your shoulder.

So here's the twist I didn't see coming. We usually assume the answer is simple: make everything quieter. But it's not quite that straightforward. First, a bit of background sound won't hurt anyone and can actually help some people concentrate — ever noticed how a café buzz helps you work? And second, silence isn't distributed fairly. The poorest neighbourhoods are almost always the loudest — they've got the motorway, the airport, the factory right on their doorstep. So noise isn't just a health issue, it's an unfairness issue. The people with the least money are the ones paying the highest price in lost sleep and lost learning. That made me properly angry, actually.

Look, I'm not saying we all need to move to the countryside and live in a soundproof bubble. That's not realistic, and honestly I'd miss the city. What I'm saying is that we should start treating noise like the health hazard it is. If you wanna protect your sleep, insist on quieter machines, better windows, sensible city planning. Measure it, regulate it, talk about it the way we talk about dirty air. Because right now, we've got a problem we can literally hear, and we've chosen not to listen. Right, thank you.

title: The Case for Doing Nothing
speaker: Aisha Karim
description: “无为”的价值：为什么我们需要真正的休息与留白
transcript:
Right, so let me ask you something. When was the last time you did absolutely nothing — and I mean nothing, no phone, no podcast, no book, just sat there? Well, if you're like most people I meet, the answer's probably never, or at least not since you were a kid. And that's what I wanna explore today.

I'm Aisha Karim, and I study rest — or, more precisely, the ways we've forgotten how to rest. And, look, I get it. We live in a culture that's obsessed with being busy. If you say you're busy, it sounds important. If you say you spent the afternoon staring out the window, you feel like you have to apologise. The moment you admit you did nothing, you feel the need to justify it, as though rest were something you had to earn or apologise for. So we've turned even our downtime into a kinda performance. Basically, we can't sit still any more.

Here's the first thing I want you to understand. Our brains aren't designed to be on all the time. When you're not focused on a task, your mind switches into what scientists call the default mode network. It's basically the brain's background setting. And in that state, something remarkable happens — your mind sorta starts wandering, you make connections between unrelated ideas, you replay conversations, you think about the future. I mean, that's where a lot of creativity actually comes from. There was a study where people did a boring task, like copying numbers, and then had to come up with new uses for everyday objects. The ones who'd been doing the boring thing came up with the most original ideas. Boredom, it turns out, is sort of a workshop for the mind. And it's not just about work — daydreaming helps you process things that happened to you, understand your own feelings, and work out what you actually want. In a way, the empty moments are when we understand ourselves best.

Now, the second point is about how we've lost that. Think about the last time you were standing in a queue or waiting for a bus. What did you do? You pulled out your phone, didn't you? We've become so uncomfortable with a few seconds of emptiness that we fill every gap with stimulation. And, um, the cost of that is subtle. We never give our minds the space to just, you know, be. It's like we're afraid of our own thoughts. And you know what? That space, once you let it in, won't stay empty for long — it fills up with the very ideas you were chasing. I dunno about you, but that strikes me as a bit sad.

So where's the surprise? Well, here's the bit that really got me. Even when we do try to rest, we tend to do it wrong. We've turned relaxation into another task. You've got yoga classes, mindfulness apps that track your 'mindfulness score', retreats where you pay a fortune to, quote, switch off. I'm not joking — people are now booking holidays organised around doing nothing, with a schedule. If your rest has a timetable and a rating, it isn't really rest, is it? You're still performing, just with a different audience. That's actually kind of ironic, if you think about it.

And here's something else that annoys me, actually. We treat rest as a reward you earn after enough work. But that's backwards. Rest isn't the prize at the end of the race; it's part of what makes the race possible. If you wait until you've finished everything to rest, you'll never rest, 'cause the list never ends. Your emails, your chores, your ambitions — they've all got a way of expanding to fill whatever time you give them. So there's always an excuse to put rest off, isn't there? I've done it myself — I'll say I'll rest once I've replied to a few emails, and then it's midnight and I'm still at my desk. Sound familiar? We're all waiting for permission that never comes.

Look, I'm not saying lie on the sofa all day and let your life fall apart. That's not rest either, and honestly it usually leaves you feeling worse. What I'm saying is that emptiness has value. So I'm gonna suggest something simple: leave a gap in your day. Go for a walk without headphones. Sit somewhere and let your attention drift. Don't turn it into a hobby, don't measure it, don't post about it. Just let it be. Because the ability to do nothing, properly, is becoming one of the rarest skills around. Thank you.

title: What Old Maps Reveal About Lost Cities
speaker: Prof. Henry Vale
description: 古地图如何帮助现代人重新发现失落的城市
transcript:
Right, so I want you to imagine you're holding a map from, say, the fifteen hundreds. The paper's yellow and stained, the ink's faded, and someone's drawn a city right there in the middle of a desert. Trouble is, nobody's ever found that city. For centuries, people assumed the map was just plain wrong — a traveller's tall tale, kinda. Well, today I want to show you why those old maps deserve a second look.

I'm Henry Vale, and I'm an archaeologist who specialises in reading old maps — well, mostly I use them to track down places that have disappeared. And, you know, there's something genuinely thrilling about it, I dunno why. A map isn't just a picture of where things are. It's a snapshot of what somebody believed, or feared, or wanted you to believe. And sometimes, hidden in the mistakes, there's a clue to a real place. Basically, every line on there is a question waiting to be asked.

Let me give you an example. There's a famous old chart — I'm gonna keep the details vague, 'cause the exact site is protected — that marked a settlement beside a river in a region now covered in sand. Everyone just sorta assumed the river had simply dried up and the town had vanished into nothing. But here's the thing, um: maps from that period were often copied from earlier maps, and copyists reproduced the same features over and over. So if a river turns up in twenty different maps, it probably wasn't somebody's mistake. It probably meant something real. And when researchers laid that old line over modern satellite images, they found the dried-up riverbed — and along it, the outlines of streets and buildings buried under the sand. I mean, the place was there the whole time. We just needed the map to know where to dig.

Now, here's a second way maps help, and this is where it gets properly clever. Old maps don't just tell you where a city sat; they show you what mattered to the people who drew them. A grand temple, a busy market, a road running off towards a mine — all of that hints at how the place was organised. So even before you lift a spade, you've got a sort of blueprint. There was a project — I think it was under jungle, somewhere in South America — where a team combined an old map with a laser survey they've flown above the forest. The laser bounced off the ground between the trees and revealed a whole network of roads and fields nobody had ever seen from below. The map supplied the question; the technology supplied the answer. You can't really do one without the other. And that, to me, is the real lesson here: the old document and the newest machine aren't rivals. They're partners, and the discovery happens in the space between them, right?

So here's the twist I love. Sometimes a map is wrong in a way that turns out to be useful. You see, a map-maker who'd never visited a place might draw it from a traveller's story, and the story might well exaggerate. But even the exaggeration tells you something. If a city's drawn three times its real size, maybe it was a centre of genuine power and wealth. If a route's drawn impossibly straight, maybe it was a road important enough to be remembered. The error itself becomes evidence. That's the bit that gets me properly excited, honestly. A mistake made five hundred years ago can point a modern archaeologist to a spot they'd otherwise walk straight past. I mean, actually, I've had that happen — followed what looked like a nonsense line on a page, and ended up standing in a field with my boots full of mud, realising the thing was right after all. You feel a bit foolish and a bit thrilled at the same time.

Look, I'm not saying every old chart is a treasure map, or that we should believe everything drawn before, like, photographs existed. Plenty of them are pure nonsense, and I won't pretend I haven't wasted weeks chasing a few. What I'm saying is that a map is a question posed by the past, and our job is to check it against the ground. Next time you see an old map in a museum, don't just admire the fancy lettering. If you wanna spot a place that isn't there anymore, ask yourself what's missing, what's been exaggerated, and what might still be out there, just waiting to be found. Thank you.

title: The Psychology of Queues
speaker: Grace Mitchell
description: 排队中的心理现象与公平感设计
transcript:
Well, right, so here's a situation I'm sure you know. You're standing in a long line at the supermarket, and the line right next to you starts moving faster. Immediately, doesn't it feel like you've picked the wrong one? Well, today I wanna talk about what's actually going on in your head when you queue — because it's far more interesting than just standing still.

I'm Grace Mitchell, and I'm a social psychologist. My work looks at the unwritten rules that govern everyday behaviour, and queuing's one of the best examples we've got. I mean, think about it: a queue is just a bunch of strangers agreeing, silently, to stand in a particular order. Nobody's in charge, and yet nearly everybody obeys. So why do we do it? And why does it wind us up so much when it goes wrong?

I mean, let's start with fairness. Here's the thing: when something's scarce, people need a rule that feels legitimate, otherwise it gets ugly. First come, first served is the rule we've settled on in most places, and we follow it even when there's no line marked on the floor. At a busy bus stop, you'll see people form a loose sort of order without anyone saying a word. And, um, if someone pushes in, the reaction's immediate and surprisingly fierce. You'll get glares, muttering, maybe a telling-off. It's not just that you've lost thirty seconds — it's that they've broken an agreement everybody else was honouring. That's why it makes you so angry, even when the delay is tiny. Basically, it's the betrayal, not the wait, that stings. And there's something else fascinating here: people will defend a line that isn't even official. If a group of us is standing loosely at a bus stop, and someone strides up and takes the front spot, you'll feel that same flash of indignation, even though nobody ever drew a line on the pavement. The rule exists because we all agree it exists. And you know, you don't have to be in a hurry to feel it.

Now here's the second idea, and this one's backed by some lovely research. It's about how we experience the waiting itself. The key finding is that occupied time feels shorter than empty time. There's a famous case in an amusement park — I'm gonna simplify it — where managers were getting complaints about long waits for a ride. They didn't actually make the wait any shorter. Instead, they put mirrors near the queue, and later little screens and games. Complaints dropped, even though people were standing there just as long. Basically, if your attention's engaged, the time slips by. 'Cause if you're just stuck there with nothing to do, every second drags, actually. I dunno about you, but I've definitely felt that. It's not about tricking people, either — it's about giving a bored mind somewhere to rest. When there's nothing to occupy you, your attention turns inward, and that's when the frustration grows.

Well, here's the twist I didn't see coming. You'd think the whole goal of queue design is to make the wait feel shorter and then send you on your way. But sometimes a queue has the opposite job. Think about the trendy café where people happily stand outside in the cold for twenty minutes. That queue isn't a problem to them — it's the point. You can't tell them it's a waste of time, 'cause to them it isn't. It signals that the place is popular, that it's worth waiting for. In a funny way, the queue becomes a kind of advertisement for itself. And online, you sorta get the same thing with virtual queues and waiting rooms for concert tickets. The wait builds anticipation, and, honestly, it might even make you value the thing more once you finally get it. Kinda strange, right? Look, I still find it odd that we'll happily pay for the privilege of standing around, but then again, I've queued for a popular bakery myself, so who am I to judge?

Look, I'm not saying every queue is a clever trick or that we should all learn to love waiting. Most queues are just badly managed, and I've cursed my share of them. What I'm saying is that the feelings they stir up — the impatience, the sense of injustice, that small pride when you get to the front — aren't random. They're built into the system. So if you're designing a service, be honest about the wait, keep it fair, and give people something to do. And if you're stuck in one, remember: the other line won't actually be faster when you switch — it just feels that way. Right, thank you.

title: Why Some Languages Are Losing Their Last Speakers
speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoye
description: 濒危语言的消失及其对文化多样性的影响
transcript:
Right, so let me begin with something a bit strange. Somewhere in the world today, there's an elderly person who is the last human being on earth who can speak a particular language. When that person dies, the language dies with them. Not gradually, not over centuries — just gone, like a light switching off. Well, that's not even a metaphor, um, actually. It's happening, you know, right now, in villages and on islands and in the back streets of big cities. That's what I want to talk about today.

I'm Samuel Okoye, and I'm a linguist. I study how languages work and why they change. But honestly, the most urgent thing in my field right now is that languages are disappearing at a rate I genuinely find alarming. We're losing, I dunno, roughly one language every two weeks. I mean, think about that. Every fortnight, a whole way of seeing the world just vanishes, and almost nobody notices.

Now, you might ask, why should we care? And look, that's a fair question. A language isn't just a set of words you can swap for another set of words. It's more like a library of knowledge that's been built up over thousands of years. When a community has lived in one place for a long time, their language encodes everything they've learned about that place — which plants are edible, how the weather changes, how to read the land. So when the language goes, all of that goes with it. It's basically like burning a library before anyone's had a chance to read the books.

Let me give you a proper example. There's a language spoken in the Amazon, and it has, well, it has an extraordinary vocabulary for the forest. It's got dozens of distinct words for different kinds of rain — the rain before a storm, the fine mist that hangs in the trees. I mean, you and I would just call all of that 'rain', right? But to a speaker of that language, those are completely different phenomena. And here's the thing: each of those words carries information that's genuinely useful for survival. Basically, the language is a survival manual disguised as grammar.

So how does a language actually die? Well, it's rarely a dramatic event. It's more of a slow drift, and this is the bit I find really sad. Usually it starts with parents making what seems like a sensible decision. They want their children to have better opportunities, so they speak the dominant language at home — the language of school, of business, of government. They're not rejecting their own tongue, you know, they're just trying to give their kids a better shot. But then the children understand the old language without speaking it, and their children don't understand it at all. Three generations, and it's over. Nobody ever made a law banning it. It just kind of evaporated.

And here's the uncomfortable part. This isn't really about geography or economics in the way people assume. It's about power. When one language has prestige — when it's the language of universities and television and money — speakers of other languages start to feel that their own tongue is somehow inferior, kinda backward. I've met people who were literally ashamed of their mother tongue, who would refuse to speak it in front of strangers. That shame is, I'd say, the real engine of language loss. It's not that the language can't survive. It's that its speakers have been convinced it doesn't deserve to.

Now, you'd expect me to end with a depressing statistic, wouldn't you? But here's the surprise, and it's the reason I still do this job. Languages can come back. There are communities that have actively revived languages that were, by every measure, basically extinct. They've done it through immersion schools, through recording the last fluent speakers, through, well, through sheer stubbornness. In some places, young people are now learning the language their grandparents were too ashamed to pass on. A language that had maybe five speakers left now has hundreds, sometimes thousands of learners. It's not easy, and it takes resources, but it proves something crucial: this isn't inevitable. If you wanna help, the first step is simply caring that it matters.

So what can you do? Well, you probably can't save a language single-handedly, and I'm not gonna pretend you can. But you can start by noticing. Notice the languages around you, the ones that don't make the news. Value them, 'cause linguistic diversity is every bit as precious as biodiversity — honestly, I'd argue more so, because a language is a living record of human thought. Next time you hear someone speaking something you don't recognise, don't think 'how odd'. Think about the extraordinary amount of knowledge packed into those sounds. Look, a world with one language would be a world with one way of thinking, and that would be a tragically poor place. Thank you.

That shame is, I'd say, the real engine of language loss.' 对应 A 的 'a sense of shame makes speakers judge their mother tongue as inferior'，是同义替换（shame → the real engine of language loss）。关键句二：'Languages can come back... through immersion schools, through recording the last fluent speakers... this isn't inevitable.' 对应 C 的 'deliberate effort through immersion schools and recordings can revive a dying language'。干扰项 B 说'政府立法禁用是主因'，与原文 'Nobody ever made a law banning it' 正面冲突，却披着'政策导致消亡'的合理外衣，最迷惑；D 说'住在偏远岛屿就能保证语言存续数百年'，原文只把岛屿列为消失发生的地点之一，'guarantees' 属无中生有且过于绝对。

title: The Truth About Multitasking
speaker: Olivia Chen
description: 多任务处理的认知代价与大脑切换成本
transcript:
Hey everyone, so here's a question I wanna start with. Raise your hand if you've ever eaten dinner while scrolling through your phone, or listened to a lecture while answering messages, or, you know, tried to hold a conversation while watching television. Right, pretty much everyone. We do this stuff all the time, and we're actually quite proud of it. We call it multitasking, like it's some kind of impressive skill. Well, today I'm gonna ruin that little illusion for you, 'cause the truth about multitasking is a lot less flattering than you might think.

I'm Olivia Chen, and I'm a cognitive scientist. Basically, I study how the brain pays attention, and let me tell you, attention is not this infinite resource you can split any way you like. It's more like a spotlight. You can point it at one thing or sweep it around fast between several, but you can't shine it on everything at once. And that distinction — between genuine parallel processing and rapid switching — is basically the whole story of multitasking.

So let me explain what's really happening in your head. When you switch from writing an email to reading a message and back, your brain doesn't just flip a switch and carry on where it left off. There's a cost. Researchers call it the switching cost, and it's basically a tiny tax you pay every single time your attention moves. You lose a bit of focus, you make more errors, and it takes your brain a moment to reload all the context of the original task. I dunno, um, maybe a few seconds each time. Sounds harmless, right? But here's the thing: those seconds add up. If you're switching every couple of minutes, you're basically paying that tax dozens of times an hour, and it quietly eats a huge chunk of your day.

Now, the research on this is genuinely striking. In one well-known study, one group worked in a solid block while another did the same work with interruptions. Well, the interrupted group took, I mean, significantly longer to finish, and they made way more mistakes. But here's the really interesting bit — they didn't realise it. The multitasking group actually believed they'd done better. They were confident, sort of certain they'd been efficient, while the evidence said the exact opposite. That gap between how well we think we're doing and how well we're actually doing is what gets me, honestly.

And it gets worse. There's evidence that heavy multitaskers are, in some ways, worse at focusing than people who rarely do it. I know, that sounds kinda backwards. You'd think practising something would make you better at it. But what you're really practising is distraction. Your brain gets very good at scanning for the next shiny thing and very bad at settling into one deep, difficult task. So the more you switch, the more your brain expects to switch, until sustained concentration starts to feel almost painful. I've seen students who literally can't read a single chapter without checking their phone every two minutes. It's not a character flaw, you know. It's a habit their brain has been trained into.

Now, you're probably wondering, is there any exception? Like, are some people genuinely good at this? And the honest answer is: almost nobody. A rare few can process two demanding tasks at once, but they're incredibly uncommon. For the rest of us, when we think we're multitasking, we're really just switching really fast and doing two things badly instead of one thing well. And, I mean, there's a special problem with digital devices, 'cause the apps are deliberately designed to pull your attention back. Every notification is a little invitation to switch. So it's not even entirely your fault — the whole system is built to interrupt you.

Here's the twist that surprised me, though. The problem isn't just that we lose time. It's what we lose in terms of the kind of thinking we're capable of. Deep, creative work — the kind that needs you to hold an idea and develop it — can't happen when you're switching every few minutes. So multitasking doesn't just make us slower. It makes our thinking shallower. We get a lot done, in a sense, but what we produce is fragmented.

So what's the practical takeaway? Well, I'm not gonna tell you to throw your phone in the bin. That's not realistic and, honestly, it's not necessary. What I'd suggest is something simpler. Try doing one thing at a time, even for short stretches, and notice how it feels. Give a conversation your full attention, or read something without a second screen. You might be surprised at how much better you focus, and, you know, how much calmer you feel. Look, attention is the raw material of everything you do. It's time we started treating it like the precious, limited thing it actually is. Thank you.

To explain why switching between tasks is not the same as true simultaneous work.
To claim that some lucky people possess an unlimited supply of mental energy.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'It's more like a spotlight. You can point it at one thing, or you can sweep it around really fast between several things, but you can't actually shine it on everything at once. And that distinction — between genuine parallel processing and rapid switching — is basically the whole story.' 推理链：聚光灯一次只能照一处→快速扫过多个目标≠同时照亮全部→真正并行与快速切换有本质区别。答案 C 的 'switching between tasks is not the same as true simultaneous work' 是对 'distinction between genuine parallel processing and rapid switching' 的直接同义替换。干扰项 A 说'注意力可自由分散'，与 'can't shine it on everything at once' 正面冲突；B 说'大脑能真正并行处理多任务'，正是讲话人要否定的误解，迷惑性最强，因为它借用了'parallel'一词；D 说'有些人拥有无限精力'，与 'not this infinite resource' 矛盾。

questions.question: In the study with interruptions, what does the speaker find most striking about the participants?

They were convinced they had performed well despite clear evidence to the contrary.
They asked to switch tasks more often because they enjoyed the variety.
They noticed immediately that interruptions were hurting their concentration.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'the interrupted group took, I mean, significantly longer to finish, and they made way more mistakes. But here's the really interesting bit — they didn't realise it. The multitasking group actually believed they'd done better... while the evidence said the exact opposite.' 题干问 'what does the speaker find most striking'，关键信号词是 'the really interesting bit'，指的就是他们误以为自己表现更好这一错觉。答案 B 的 'convinced they had performed well despite clear evidence to the contrary' 精准概括 'believed they'd done better... evidence said the exact opposite'。干扰项 A 说'他们比 uninterrupted 组完成得更快'，与 'significantly longer' 方向相反，是最典型的数字/方向对调陷阱；C 说'因喜欢变化而要求多切换'，原文无此动机；D 说'立刻察觉到分心影响'，与 'they didn't realise it' 直接矛盾。

questions.question: What does the speaker imply when she says heavy multitaskers are practising distraction rather than skill?
options: Regular switching actually strengthens the brain's ability to concentrate deeply.
The brain eventually adapts so that switching becomes completely effortless.
Students who switch tasks are simply lacking in natural intelligence and willpower.
Frequent task-switching trains the mind to crave novelty and resist sustained effort.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'what you're really practising is distraction. Your brain gets very good at scanning for the next shiny thing and very bad at settling into one deep, difficult task... the more your brain expects to switch.' 推理链：反复切换=练习分心→大脑擅长寻找新鲜刺激、不擅长深入→越切越想切。答案 D 的 'trains the mind to crave novelty and resist sustained effort' 正是对 'scanning for the next shiny thing / bad at settling into deep task' 的言外之意概括。干扰项 A 说'切换能增强专注力'与原文 'worse at focusing' 直接相反，是迷惑性最强项；B 说'大脑最终完全毫不费力地适应切换'，原文反而说 concentration 变得痛苦，方向相反；C 把问题归为'智力或意志力缺陷'，而讲话人明确说 'It's not a character flaw... a habit their brain has been trained into'，正面冲突。

questions.question: According to the speaker, which TWO costs of multitasking are supported by the research she cites? (Choose TWO)

Interruptions make people take longer and produce more errors than steady work.
People who multitask accurately judge how much their performance has suffered.

questions.explanation: 本题要求跨段落归纳多任务处理的代价。音频关键句一：'it's basically a tiny tax you pay every single time your attention moves... those seconds add up... quietly eats a huge chunk of your day.' 对应 A 的 'small penalties that accumulate into lost time'（tax → penalties，add up → accumulate，同义替换）。关键句二：'the interrupted group took significantly longer to finish, and they made way more mistakes.' 对应 B 的 'take longer and produce more errors than steady work'。干扰项 C 说'多任务者能准确判断自己表现下滑'，与 'they didn't realise it... believed they'd done better' 正面冲突，它借用'performance'一词制造迷惑；D 说'频繁切换保证让人更擅长深度创造性工作'，与 'makes our thinking shallower' 完全相反，属于方向对调。

title: How Gardens Changed the Way We Eat
speaker: Jack Foster
description: 家庭菜园的历史演变及其对饮食观念的影响
transcript:
G'day everyone. Right, so I want you to think about the last meal you ate. Go on, picture it. Where did it come from? Chances are it came from a supermarket, in a packet, and it travelled a long way to reach your plate. Well, that's so normal to us now that we barely think about it. But it's actually a very recent invention. For most of human history, the food on your plate came from somewhere you could walk to. And the place that changed all of that, the place that quietly revolutionised how we eat, was the humble garden. That's what I wanna talk about today.

I'm Jack Foster, and I'm a food historian. Basically, I study the story of what people eat and how that's changed over time. And, you know, when you look back, the garden isn't just a patch of vegetables. It's more like a reflection of how a society thinks about food, about work, about the land. I mean, the way a culture gardens tells you a lot about what that culture values. Trace that story and you'll see how our relationship with food shifted, from producing it ourselves to mostly buying it.

Let's go back a bit. For thousands of years, a garden was a matter of survival, not a hobby. You know, you grew what you needed to eat, simple as that. Households had a small plot for vegetables, a few chickens, maybe a fruit tree. And the Garden of Eden idea, you know, that deep cultural story about a perfect garden — well, that tells you how central gardens were to the way people imagined a good life. It was basically the original dream of abundance, where food was free and plentiful.

Right, here's where it gets interesting. As people moved into towns, they couldn't grow their own food any more. So food started to become a commodity — something produced by someone else and sold to you. And this is where the garden starts to take on a different role. It's no longer strictly necessary, but people keep them anyway, 'cause there's something deeply satisfying about growing your own. I dunno, um, maybe it's the connection to the seasons, or just the pride of eating something you made yourself. That's the bit that never really went away.

So, look, let me give you a concrete example. During the Second World War, lots of countries had serious food shortages, and governments encouraged people to grow vegetables in any spare patch of land they could find. These were called victory gardens, and, well, they were everywhere — in backyards, in parks, even on the roofs of buildings. And here's the remarkable thing: those gardens produced an enormous amount of food — a significant share of the vegetables people ate. But, I mean, when the war ended and food became readily available again, most people gave them up. The moment the necessity disappeared, the gardens disappeared with it. That tells you something about how we treat food, doesn't it?

Well, the unexpected part of the story is what happened next. Once industrial farming took over, food got cheaper and more plentiful than ever before. But something was lost. When you grow food, you're connected to the process — you plant, you wait, you watch the weather, you harvest. And that connection shapes how you value what's on your plate. But when food arrives in a clean packet with no dirt on it, you lose that sense of where it came from. I've spoken to kids who genuinely believe vegetables grow in supermarkets. It's not their fault, you know. I kinda feel sorry for them, honestly. It's just that the garden — the living proof of how food is made — has vanished from their experience.

And here's a twist I didn't expect when I started this research. The garden is actually making a comeback, but in a new form. Community gardens are springing up in cities all over the world. People rent a small plot, grow things together, and, well, rediscover that old satisfaction. And it's not really about saving money — you can buy a carrot far cheaper than you can grow one. It's about something else. It's about connection, and community, and, sort of, remembering that food has a story. Researchers have found that people who garden eat more vegetables, even young people. Basically, growing food changes what you want to eat.

So what's the lesson here? Well, I'm not gonna tell you all to dig up your lawns and plant cabbages. Look, I'm a historian, not a gardener, and honestly my own attempts at growing tomatoes were pretty disastrous. But I'd suggest you think about where your food comes from, even a little. Notice the distance it travelled, the hands that grew it. 'Cause the garden taught us something important, and we're in danger of forgetting it: food isn't just fuel you buy. It's a relationship with the land and with the seasons and with each other. Thank you very much.

questions.question: Why does the speaker mention the Garden of Eden when discussing the role of gardens?
options: To argue that ancient myths exaggerate how difficult growing food really was.
To show that gardens have long stood for an ideal of plenty and a good life.

It was basically the original dream of abundance.' 推理链：伊甸园是'完美花园'的文化故事→说明花园在人们想象美好生活中居于核心→是'富足的原始梦想'。答案 B 的 'gardens have long stood for an ideal of plenty and a good life' 是对 'dream of abundance / central to imagining a good life' 的同义替换（plenty 对应 abundance，ideal 对应 imagined）。干扰项 A 说'神话夸大种地难度'，原文无此批判；C 说'超市终于造出了人间完美花园'，与全文'超市让我们失去与食物的联系'相反；D 说'宗教分散了人们对实用农耕的注意'，纯属无中生有，是借'Garden of Eden'外衣编造的迷惑项。

questions.question: What does the story of victory gardens suggest about people's relationship with growing food?
options: People eagerly kept growing their own vegetables long after the war had finished.
The government had to force reluctant citizens to cultivate spare patches of land.
Growing food was embraced out of necessity and abandoned once that need passed.

But when the war ended and food became readily available again, most people gave them up. The moment the necessity disappeared, the gardens disappeared with it.' 推理链：战争造成短缺→种菜出于必要→战后必要消失→花园随之消失。答案 C 的 'growing food was embraced out of necessity and abandoned once that need passed' 精准对应 'the moment the necessity disappeared, the gardens disappeared'。干扰项 A 说'战后仍热忠于自种'与 'most people gave them up' 直接相反；B 说'政府强迫不情愿的市民'与 'encouraged' 语气不符，且原文无'不情愿'；D 说'屋顶花园比地面菜园产量更高'，原文只把屋顶列为地点之一（even on the roofs），未作产量比较，属于借原文词汇的迷惑项。

questions.question: What does the speaker imply about children who think vegetables grow in supermarkets?
options: They are unusually curious about how industrial farming actually works.
They have been cut off from the process that shows where food truly originates.
They know more about nutrition than the adults who shop for them.
They would grow vegetables themselves if only their schools allowed it.

I've spoken to kids who genuinely believe vegetables grow in supermarkets. It's not their fault, you know... the garden — the living proof of how food is made — has vanished from their experience.' 推理链：洁净包装切断了来源感→孩子误以为蔬菜长在超市→因为花园从他们生活中消失。答案 B 的 'they have been cut off from the process that shows where food truly originates' 是对 'lose that sense of where it came from / vanished from their experience' 的言外之意概括。干扰项 A 说'他们对工业农业格外好奇'，与原文'误以为长在超市'的无知相反；C 说'比大人更懂营养'，原文无比较；D 说'只要学校允许就会自己种菜'，属于无中生有的假设，迷惑性在于它披着'孩子'话题的外衣。

questions.question: According to the speaker, which TWO changes did industrial farming bring about in how people view food? (Choose TWO)
options: It made food cheaper and more abundant than at any previous time in history.

title: The Quiet Power of Boredom
speaker: Dr. Elena Rossi
description: 无聊如何激发创造力与自我反思
transcript:
Right, so I want to start with a confession. The other day I was stuck on a train, no signal, nothing to read, just sitting with my own thoughts for forty minutes. At first I was, well, climbing the walls. I felt genuinely uncomfortable. But somewhere in the middle of that journey, something odd happened. An idea I'd been struggling with for weeks suddenly clicked into place. And, you know, that wasn't a coincidence. Today I wanna talk about why being bored — properly, deeply bored — might be one of the most useful things you can be.

I'm Elena Rossi, and I'm a psychologist interested in creativity and how the mind wanders. Now, we live in a world that's basically obsessed with avoiding boredom. There's always a screen to scroll or a podcast to fill the silence. And we treat that as a good thing, don't we? We think, right, I'm never bored, I'm always productive. I mean, boredom has a reputation problem, and I'd like to change that.

Let me explain what boredom really is. It's not just 'nothing to do'. It's a mental state where you want to be engaged but find nothing worth engaging with. And that feeling of restlessness, of mild frustration — well, it's actually a signal. It's your brain saying, 'I need something meaningful, and I can't find it here.' So the mind starts to search. And when there's no external entertainment to grab your attention, the brain turns inward. It starts daydreaming, connecting ideas, running simulations. Basically, boredom pushes your attention from the outside world to your own internal world. And that, it turns out, is where a lot of creativity lives.

Here's a proper example. A famous mathematician got the key insight to a hard problem while, of all things, staring out of a window on a boring train. I mean, he wasn't working on it at that moment. He'd, uh, stopped consciously thinking about it. His mind was still working in the background, making connections he couldn't make while concentrating hard. And then, when he let his guard down, the answer just popped into his head. That's not magic. That's what the wandering mind does. You know, we've all had that experience of getting a great idea in the shower, right? The shower is boring, so your mind is free to roam.

Now, the research backs this up. There was a study where they gave people a really dull task — copying numbers out of a phone book. And then, afterwards, they gave them a creativity test. Well, the people who'd done the boring task came up with more original ideas than the group who'd done an interesting task instead. I dunno if you find that as surprising as I do, but it suggests that boredom isn't the enemy of creativity. It might be, sort of, its fuel. The dullness clears space for original thinking.

But here's where it gets tricky, and this is the bit I want you to really hear. There are two kinds of boredom, and only one of them is useful. There's 'dead-end boredom', where you're stuck and frustrated and feel awful — that's not helpful. But then there's 'open boredom', where you're not suffering, you're just kinda available. Your mind has room to breathe. And the difference, basically, comes down to whether you fill the space or let it be. The moment we feel a flicker of boredom, we reach for a device; we can't stand the emptiness. And in doing that, we're basically closing the door on that creative space before it's had a chance to open.

Now, you might be thinking, well, surely constant stimulation makes us smarter, doesn't it? And here's the unexpected finding. It doesn't. In fact, constantly filling every gap seems to make us worse at reflecting on our own experience. How often do you sit and think about your day without something playing in the background? Honestly, most of us almost never do. We're so busy consuming content that we've forgotten how to be with our own thoughts. And that's a real loss, 'cause reflection is how we make sense of our lives, how we learn from what happened to us. Without it, we just keep moving without ever really processing anything.

So what's the practical advice? Well, I'm not gonna ask you to give up your phone forever. Look, that's not going to happen, and I'm not even sure it'd be good for you. What I'd suggest is small. Leave a little gap in your day. Walk somewhere without headphones. Sit on a bus and just look out of the window. Let yourself be bored for five minutes and see what your mind does. You might find it uncomfortable at first, but you might also find, like I did, that something interesting shows up. Look, boredom isn't a waste of time. It's one of the few spaces left where your mind can actually be your own. Thank you.

questions.question: What does the speaker's opening story about being stuck on a train mainly serve to demonstrate?

That a spell of enforced boredom can unexpectedly unlock a stuck idea.

questions.question: According to the speaker, what mechanism explains why boredom can help creativity?

Basically, boredom pushes your attention from the outside world to your own internal world.' 答案 D 的 'removes outside distractions so the mind turns inward and connects ideas' 精准对应 'no external entertainment... brain turns inward... connecting ideas'。干扰项 A 说'迫使大脑更努力处理手头任务'与原文'停止有意识思考、转向内心'不符；B 说'训练人忽略挫败感直到消失'，原文承认无聊就是 mild frustration 的信号，并未教人忽略；C 说'提供持续不断的外部新信息'与 'no external entertainment' 完全相反，是方向对调的强干扰项。

questions.question: What does the speaker imply about the difference between 'dead-end' and 'open' boredom?
options: Both kinds are equally valuable as long as the mind is left completely idle.
Only the distressed, frustrated form creates the space needed for new ideas.
The useful kind leaves room to breathe, while the painful kind merely traps us.
Filling every empty moment is the surest way to reach the creative state.
questions.explanation: 音频关键句：'There's what I'd call dead-end boredom, where you're stuck and frustrated and you just feel awful — that's not helpful. But then there's open boredom, where you're not suffering, you're just kinda available. Your mind has room to breathe... it comes down to whether you fill the space or let it be.' 推理链：dead-end=痛苦被困（无益）→ open=不痛苦、有余地（有益）→差别在于是否填满空间。答案 C 的 'the useful kind leaves room to breathe, while the painful kind merely traps us' 是对 'room to breathe / stuck and frustrated' 的言外之意概括。干扰项 A 说'两种都有价值只要彻底放空'与 'that's not helpful' 冲突；B 说'只有痛苦的那种才能创造空间'，正好说反；D 说'填满每个空档最能进入创造状态'与 'we're closing the door on that creative space' 完全相反。

questions.question: According to the speaker, which TWO findings support the idea that boredom benefits thinking? (Choose TWO)
options: People given a dull copying task later produced more original ideas than others.

A wandering mind can form connections that focused concentration cannot manage.
People who avoid all boredom report the highest levels of daily creativity.
questions.explanation: 本题要求跨段落归纳'无聊有益'的证据。音频关键句一：'the people who'd done the boring task came up with more original ideas than the group who'd done an interesting task' 对应 A 的 'dull copying task later produced more original ideas'（boring task → dull copying task，同义替换）。关键句二：'his mind was still quietly working in the background, making connections he couldn't make when he was concentrating hard' 对应 C 的 'a wandering mind can form connections that focused concentration cannot manage'。干扰项 B 说'填满每个空档让人更善于反思'，与 'constantly filling every gap seems to make us worse at reflecting' 正面冲突，方向反用；D 说'完全不无聊的人创造力最高'，与全文主旨相反，是披着'creativity'外衣的强迷惑项。

title: Why We Trust Strangers Online
speaker: Nathaniel Reed
description: 在线信任的机制：我们为何相信陌生人及平台设计的影响
transcript:
Hey everyone, so let me start with something that'll make you think. When was the last time you got into a car with a driver you'd never met before? Or let a stranger into your home to stay for a weekend? Or, you know, handed over your money to someone whose real name you didn't even know? Well, if you've used a ride-sharing app, a homestay service, or an online marketplace, you've done all three. And here's the strange thing: you probably didn't think twice about it. Today I wanna look at why we trust strangers online, and what that says about us.

I'm Nathaniel Reed, and I study trust in digital societies. Basically, I study how people decide whom to believe when they can't see or meet the other person. And, you know, for most of human history, trust was a local thing. You trusted your family, neighbours and village; everyone knew everyone, and reputation travelled by word of mouth. If someone cheated you, the whole community knew about it by dinner time. But the internet has completely upended that. Now we deal with people we'll never meet, and, well, we do it with remarkable confidence. So how exactly does that work?

Let me give you the classic example. You book a room through a website. You've never met the host or seen the house, yet you hand over a significant amount of money. Why? Well, um, mostly because of the review system. You can read what dozens of previous guests said. They rated it, described it, left photos. And those reviews, I mean, they do the job that gossip used to do in a village. They make the stranger accountable. 'Cause here's the thing: a host who knows their reputation is public has a strong reason to behave well. One bad review can hurt their business. So the system basically manufactures trust out of information.

Now, here's where it gets interesting, and this is the part I find genuinely fascinating. Research shows we read reviews in a very particular, sort of irrational way. We trust detailed, specific reviews far more than short positive ones. A review that says 'great place, loved it' doesn't convince us much. But one that mentions the squeaky door and the excellent coffee? Well, that feels honest, 'cause real people notice small details. I dunno, maybe we assume that someone who bothers to write a lot must be telling the truth. And here's the kicker — we're often right about that, but the system also has serious weaknesses.

Because, obviously, reviews can be faked: sellers write glowing reviews of their own products or pay others to do it. And, you know, the platforms know this, so they've built detection systems to spot suspicious patterns. But it's a bit of an arms race, honestly. As the platforms get better at catching fakes, the fakes get better at looking real. And the worrying thing is that most users, well, they can't tell the difference. I've shown people fake reviews and real ones side by side, and they're basically guessing. So a lot of the trust we place in these systems is, sort of, misplaced. We feel informed, but we might just be confidently wrong.

Here's an unexpected finding that changed how I think about this. The design of the platform matters more than the actual information. In one study, researchers created two versions of the same marketplace. One looked professional and polished, with nice photos and clean layout. The other had identical content but looked amateurish and cluttered. Well, people trusted the polished one far more, even though the information — the prices, the descriptions, the ratings — was exactly the same. I mean, that's not rational. But it tells you something important: our trust is partly an emotional response to design, not a careful judgement of evidence. We're kinda wired to equate good-looking with trustworthy.

And here's the deeper point. This design-driven trust has a dark side. They decide what information you see and which reviews get shown first. So when you say 'I trust this seller', really you're trusting the platform's judgment, and, well, that's a very different thing. 'Cause the platform has its own interests, which don't always match yours. I'm not saying they're evil, you know — most of them aren't. Their goal is keeping you on the site and making transactions happen, which isn't quite the same as getting you the best deal.

So where does that leave us? Well, I'm not gonna tell you to stop trusting strangers online. That'd be absurd — the whole system works, and it's brought real benefits. What I'd suggest is that you trust with your eyes open. Look for the details in reviews, not just the star rating. Notice when a site is trying to impress you with polish. And remember that the platform is not a neutral referee; it's a business. Look, trust is the glue that holds modern life together, and online it's more fragile than it looks. A little healthy suspicion, honestly, goes a long way. Thank you.

Their trust is shaped more by surface appearance than by the actual evidence.
